content: The sclera is the opaque, typically white, fibrous, and protective outer layer of the eye. It is composed of collagen and elastic fibers, which contribute to its structural integrity. In children, the sclera is thinner, allowing some of the underlying pigment to show through, giving it a slightly bluish appearance. In elderly individuals, fatty deposits can accumulate on the sclera, causing it to appear slightly yellow. The sclera constitutes the posterior five-sixths of the connective tissue layer of the eyeball. It plays a critical role in maintaining the shape of the globe, providing resistance to both internal and external forces. Additionally, it serves as the site of attachment for the extraocular muscles, which are responsible for eye movement. These muscle insertions are located approximately 3 millimeters behind the rectus muscle attachments. Additional anatomical features include the interior view of the anterior half of the eyeball, the terminal portion of the optic nerve and its entry into the eyeball in a horizontal section, and the interior of the posterior half of the left eyeball.
